meta.title: Privacy and Data Governance
meta.thesis: Privacy and Data Governance is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A support assistant handles account details and must minimize, retain, and delete data correctly. By the end, they should be able to build or review privacy data-flow map with collection, retention, and deletion rules, measure sensitive fields handled according to policy, and catch the failure where logs keep personal data long after the user request is resolved.

blocks.title: The breach surface is often the log

spans.text: Problem anchor: a learner pastes a transcript containing names, grades, and health context into a lesson coach. The app sends it to a model, stores a trace, embeds a summary for memory, logs an error, and later includes the example in an eval set. Privacy review must follow all of those copies.

A data inventory names each surface: user input, uploaded files, retrieval chunks, embeddings, model request, model output, trace, analytics event, support ticket, eval dataset, cache, vendor system, and deletion workflow.

Field: learner free-text prompt. Classification: personal data possible, credentials possible, minors data possible depending on deployment. Use: generate coaching response. Stored: trace metadata by default; raw text only with explicit debug mode and redaction. Vendor: approved model route only. Retention: 30 days for raw debug traces, aggregate metrics longer. Deletion: trace, cache, memory, and vector derivatives included.

modules.summary: The strongest privacy control is not collecting or retaining sensitive data unnecessarily.
objectives: Classify AI workflow data by sensitivity.

blocks.title: Do not make redaction your only plan

spans.text: PII detection is useful but imperfect. Privacy governance should first ask whether the data is needed at all. If a lesson coach does not need phone numbers, credentials, exact birth dates, or medical details, block or redact them before storage and avoid sending them to vendors unnecessarily.

Moderation classifies content risk; PII controls classify personal data; governance decides retention, access, consent, deletion, and review authority. Treat them as related layers, not one magic filter.

blocks.title: Case study: vector store deletion gap

spans.text: A school deletes a document containing student names. The source file disappears, but chunks and embeddings remain in the retrieval index. The app can still surface the content indirectly. A real deletion workflow must remove source, chunks, embeddings, cache entries, and trace references according to policy.

modules.title: Govern vendors, access, and retention
modules.sub: Control who can see raw data, where it goes, and how long it survives.
modules.summary: AI privacy governance lives in vendor settings, access controls, retention tables, and audit events.
objectives: Tie policy versions to audit logs.

blocks.title: Every copy needs an owner and timer

spans.text: A model request may leave your infrastructure; a trace may be readable by engineers; an eval set may be shared with contractors; a vector store may outlive the source. Privacy governance assigns owners, access levels, retention periods, and deletion procedures to each copy.

Vendor review should cover data-use settings, retention, subprocessors, region, logging, support access, model training use, incident notification, and deletion support. The product should log policy version and redaction action so later reviewers know what happened.

Raw learner prompts: store only when debug sampling is enabled, redact obvious PII and secrets, retain 30 days, access limited to trust-and-safety reviewers. Trace metadata: retain 180 days for reliability and cost monitoring. Aggregated quality metrics: retain longer without raw text. Vector memory: disabled for school tenants unless explicit agreement covers purpose, retention, and deletion.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Prefer metadata and aggregates when raw text is not necessary.
blocks.useWhen: Use raw content capture only for clear debugging, safety review, or user-support purposes with access and retention limits.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid broad trace access, indefinite prompt retention, or vendor routing that conflicts with data classification.

blocks.title: Prompt handling gate sketch

spans.text: This is deliberately simple. It demonstrates the control points: block secrets, redact before model calls or logs, and record the policy action for later review.

predictThenReveal.answer: Raw prompts can contain sensitive personal data, so default metadata logging is safer unless a justified debug or review workflow exists.

blocks.title: Verify an AI-generated data governance plan

spans.text: Check that generated plans include a data inventory, classification, minimization, retention, deletion, access control, vendor routing, raw-trace policy, vector-store deletion, eval-set governance, and incident review. Reject plans that say "we redact PII" without explaining when, where, and how failures are handled.

objectives: Write a retrieval prompt for future reviews.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "How do I govern data in an AI workflow?" Include inventory, classification, minimization, redaction, vendor review, access, retention, deletion, traces, embeddings, evals, audit logs, and incident review.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Treat data governance as infrastructure, not policy prose.
blocks.useWhen: Use formal governance when prompts, documents, traces, embeddings, or tools may contain personal, confidential, regulated, or learner-sensitive data.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid launching memory, analytics, or eval reuse features before deletion and access rules are defined.

blocks.title: Capstone: create a data surface map

spans.text: Pick one AI feature. Draw a table with every data surface, sensitivity class, purpose, vendor, storage location, retention, access group, deletion path, and audit event. Then choose one surface to minimize or eliminate before launch.

hallucination.label: Hallucination
hallucination.technicalNote: Privacy harm can occur when a hallucination invents personal facts or exposes inferred sensitive attributes.

prompt_injection.label: Prompt injection
prompt_injection.laymanDefinition: An attack that can attempt to extract or move sensitive data.
prompt_injection.technicalNote: Injection defenses are part of privacy governance when untrusted text can trigger disclosure through model output or tools.

guardrail.label: Guardrail
guardrail.laymanDefinition: A data-control rule enforced in product or infrastructure.
guardrail.technicalNote: Privacy guardrails include minimization, redaction, access control, retention, vendor routing, deletion, and audit logs.

privacy.label: Privacy
privacy.laymanDefinition: The practice of limiting, protecting, and governing personal or sensitive data.
privacy.technicalNote: In AI systems, privacy applies to prompts, files, embeddings, logs, traces, eval sets, vendor calls, and support tooling.

owasp.label: OWASP
owasp.laymanDefinition: A security lens that includes sensitive information disclosure.
owasp.technicalNote: OWASP complements privacy governance by highlighting prompt, output, plugin, and vector-store leakage paths.

risk_register.label: Risk register
risk_register.laymanDefinition: A record of privacy risks, controls, owners, and residual exposure.
risk_register.technicalNote: Data inventory findings should feed the risk register with retention, access, vendor, and deletion decisions.

questions.q: What decision does Privacy and Data Governance change for this case?
questions.why: A good lesson changes how the learner builds, reviews, or ships privacy data-flow map with collection, retention, and deletion rules.
questions.rot: Choose the smallest option that catches: logs keep personal data long after the user request is resolved.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct AI privacy governance: inventory data, classify sensitivity, minimize before prompts and logs, control vendor and access paths, define retention and deletion, audit actions, and review incidents.
